title: Discipling Through Suffering
subtitle: Five sessions on walking with someone whose life is falling apart
summary: Someone you love is falling apart, and you do not know what to say. This study is for that moment. It is five sessions on the ministry almost no one teaches, walking with a person through grief, illness, loss, or a season of darkness, without lying to them and without leaving them alone. It begins where the friends of Job began, in silence on the ground. It learns the language of lament from the Psalms, refuses the cruelty of tidy answers, meets the God who suffered on a cross, and ends in a hope honest enough to hold real tears. Along the way it keeps a path to professional help in plain view, because some darkness is heavier than friendship alone can carry.
setting: A table for the brokenhearted. No fixing allowed. Presence first.
forWho: Anyone discipling or befriending a person in grief, illness, loss, or a season of darkness, and unsure what to say.
rhythm: Five sessions, gentle and slow, with long silences allowed. Sometimes the session is just being there.
leaderNote: The most common mistake is talking too soon. The friends of Job were wisest in the seven silent days and foolish the moment they opened their mouths to explain. Teach the disciple-maker to sit, to weep, to stay, and to keep a real path to professional help in view. Do not validate despair, and do not rush past the pain to a verse. If the person you are walking with is sinking into a darkness that frightens you, get a pastor or a counselor into the room. Some weight is not meant to be carried by friendship alone.

sessions.title: Sit in the Ashes First
sessions.bigIdea: The friends of Job did their finest work in silence. For seven days they sat on the ground and said nothing, and it was the truest comfort they ever gave. Presence comes before words, and often it is the whole gift.
sessions.open: Think of a time your own world came apart. Who showed up. Not who said the right thing, but who simply came and stayed.
sessions.read: Read Job 2:11-13 slowly. Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him. And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven. And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
observe: How long did the friends sit before anyone spoke. Count the days named in the passage.
What did they do with their bodies before they did anything with their mouths. List the actions.
talk: The friends of Job are famous for being wrong, but that came later, when they opened their mouths to explain his pain. Here, at the start, they get it exactly right. What is the difference between the silence in verse 13 and the speeches that ruined everything after.

Most of us talk too soon at a hospital bed or a graveside because the silence frightens us. Be honest at this table. What are we actually afraid of when we sit with someone in pain, and who is that fear really serving.
There is a person you know right now whose life is coming apart. What would it cost you this week to go and simply sit with them, bringing no answers.
sessions.practice: Go and be present to one hurting person this week. Do not bring a lesson or a verse ready to fire. Bring your body and your time. Sit, listen, and let the silence be long. If they want to talk, follow where they lead. If they do not, staying is enough.
sessions.send: You do not have to explain their pain to be a comfort in it. You only have to come, and stay.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other person in your circle that someone is hurting, and ask them to go too. Grief needs more than one friend, and the person who taught you to sit quietly can teach the next.

sessions.title: Give Them the Language of Lament
sessions.bigIdea: The Psalms hand the suffering a vocabulary the church often hides from them. How long, O LORD. Half the Psalms complain to God out loud, and heaven never once tells them to be quiet. Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith, refusing to pretend.
sessions.open: When you were a child and something hurt, were you allowed to say so out loud in your house, or were you taught to keep it in and put on a face.
sessions.read: Read Psalm 13 together. How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me? Consider and answer me, O LORD my God. Light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, I have prevailed over him, lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken. But I have trusted in your steadfast love. My heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.
observe: Count how many times the phrase how long appears in the first two verses. What does that repetition tell you about the state of the writer.
The psalm does not end where it began. What has changed by the last two verses, and what has not changed.
talk: David asks God how long, and even accuses God of hiding his face, and this is in the church's own prayer book. Why do you think we so rarely let a grieving person pray like this out loud.

Notice what the psalm does not do. It does not deny the pain, and it does not stay in it forever either. It travels from complaint to trust without skipping the complaint. Why is skipping the complaint so tempting, and what does it cost the sufferer when we make them skip it.
When someone we love is angry at God, we often rush to defend God. What would it mean instead to hand them Psalm 13 and tell them this prayer is allowed.
sessions.practice: This week, give a grieving friend permission to be honest with God. You might read Psalm 13 together, or you might simply say out loud that God can hold their anger and their questions. Do not correct their lament. Sit inside it with them and let them say the true thing.
sessions.send: The shortest road out of the dark is not around the pain. It is straight through it, out loud, to a God who does not flinch.
sessions.passItOn: Teach one other person that lament belongs in prayer. Show them Psalm 13. A friend who learns that complaint is allowed becomes a friend who can sit with the next sufferer without panic.

sessions.title: Do Not Explain It Away
sessions.bigIdea: Paul does not say fix those who weep, or correct those who weep. He says weep with them. And when Jesus stood at a grave he already knew he would empty, he still wept. The tidy answer is a cruelty dressed as help. Tears are the truer theology.
sessions.open: What is the worst thing anyone said to you when you were grieving, some line that was meant to help and only made it hurt more.
sessions.read: Read Romans 12:15. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Then read John 11:33-35, at the grave of Lazarus. When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, Where have you laid him? They said to him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept.
observe: Jesus was minutes away from raising Lazarus from the dead. Knowing that, what is remarkable about the fact that he still wept.
Paul gives a command in Romans 12:15. Is weeping with someone presented as an optional kindness or as an instruction.
talk: Everything in us wants to answer the question why did this happen. Jesus, who actually knew the answer and the ending, did not lead with it. He wept first. What does that teach us about the timing of explanations.

The tidy answers we reach for, they are in a better place, everything happens for a reason, God needed another angel, are meant to comfort. Say honestly why they so often wound instead. Whose discomfort are they really soothing.

This is hard, so name it plainly. A grieving person carrying real despair may need more than any of us can give. How do we weep with someone and also help them reach a pastor or a counselor when the darkness is more than friendship can hold.
sessions.practice: Refuse one tidy answer this week. When you are with someone in pain, resist the reflex to explain or to find a silver lining. Say I am so sorry, and I am here, and then stop talking. If their grief is turning to a despair that frightens you, gently help them get to a pastor or a professional. Weeping with someone and pointing them toward real help are the same love.
sessions.send: Do not answer a grief that only asks to be shared. Weep first. The explanation can wait, and it may never be yours to give.
sessions.passItOn: Free one other person from the pressure to have answers. Tell them the most Christlike thing at a graveside is often tears and not sentences. That permission spreads from one comforter to the next.

sessions.title: The God Who Suffered
sessions.bigIdea: The cross means our God is not watching pain from a safe distance. He entered it. A man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, a high priest tempted in every way we are. Whatever else suffering means, it does not mean God stayed away.
sessions.open: When you are in real pain, does God feel near or far. Answer honestly. There is no correct answer at this table.
sessions.read: Read Isaiah 53:3-5. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief. And as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed. Then read Hebrews 4:15. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
observe: Isaiah 53 piles up words for pain, sorrows, grief, despised, pierced, crushed. Who is the passage saying carries all of that.
Hebrews says our high priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses. What reason does the verse give for why he can.
talk: Many people walk away from God over suffering, and it is an honest reason to walk. Here is what the cross puts on the table. Our God has scars. How does a suffering God change the question, even if it does not answer all of it.

Isaiah says he was pierced for our transgressions and by his stripes we are healed. This is not a God who explains our pain from the clouds. He bleeds inside it. What comfort is there in a God who suffered, that a God who merely rules could not give.

We cannot tell a sufferer exactly why their particular pain came. But we can tell them where God is in it. Practice saying that out loud right now. What would you actually say to someone who asks where God is in this.
sessions.practice: Sit with the wounds of Jesus this week, on your own and with the one you are walking beside. You do not need to solve the problem of pain. You need to know, and to help another person know, that Jesus is not far off from it. When they ask where God is, you can point to a cross and say he is here, in it with you.
sessions.send: We do not follow a God who stayed clean and dry above our grief. We follow one with holes in his hands.
sessions.passItOn: Carry this to one more person who thinks suffering proves God is absent or uncaring. You will not win the argument with cleverness. Show them the scars, and let the God who suffered speak for himself.

sessions.title: Hope That Does Not Lie
sessions.bigIdea: Paul does not tell the grieving to stop grieving. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope. Grief and hope live in the same house here. Resurrection is not the denial of death. It is the promise that death does not get the last word, and one day every tear gets wiped away.
sessions.open: What does false hope sound like to you, the cheerful kind that skips the pain. And have you ever been handed it in a hard season.
sessions.read: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13. But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope. Then read Revelation 21:4. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away.
observe: Paul does not forbid grief. Read the verse again. What exactly is the kind of grief he warns against.
In Revelation 21:4, notice the tears are still there to be wiped. What does that say about how honest this hope is about pain.
talk: There is a false comfort that tells the grieving to cheer up because heaven is real, and it lands like a slap. How is the hope of Revelation 21 different from that. Where does it make room for the tears.

Paul says grieve, but not as those with no hope. So Christian hope does not cancel sorrow. It refuses to let sorrow be the final word. Why does it matter that we keep both, the honest grief and the real hope, and not trade one for the other.

We have walked five sessions, from silence to lament to weeping to the God who suffered, and now to hope. Who in your life needs you to walk this whole road with them. Name them, and say what the first step is.
sessions.practice: Speak honest hope to one grieving person this week. Not the hope that hurries them past their tears, but the hope that sits with the tears and promises they will not last forever. Say death does not get the last word, and mean it, and do not use it to shut down their sorrow. If their grief has become a darkness that scares you or them, make sure a pastor or a counselor is walking with them too.
sessions.send: The tears are real, and they are counted, and there is a hand that will wipe every one of them away. Grieve, but not like someone with nothing coming.
sessions.passItOn: Hand this whole road to one more person. Teach someone else to sit, to lament, to weep, to point to the God who suffered, and to speak hope that does not lie. The best comfort you were given is meant to be given again.
